title: C DSA implementation safety: bounds, ownership and invariants
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its constraints.
Trace the example and reason about its data flow.
Identify complexity, boundary or safety considerations.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Data structures rely on invariants such as valid array bounds, correct list links, unique ownership and consistent tree ordering. Every operation must preserve those invariants on both success and failure paths.
understand.whyItMatters: A data structure that works for ordinary inputs may still fail on empty, full, malformed or allocation-failure cases. Invariants provide a systematic way to reason about correctness.
understand.analogy: Treat an algorithm or data structure as a set of operations that must preserve a clearly stated contract.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace formal complexity analysis, C object rules or algorithm preconditions.

explain.narrative:
Data structures rely on invariants such as valid array bounds, correct list links, unique ownership and consistent tree ordering. Every operation must preserve those invariants on both success and failure paths.

Before implementation, state input constraints, empty-case behaviour, ownership and invariants. Compile with warnings and test representative, boundary and failure cases.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The function checks pointers and capacity before writing. It increments count only after the new value has been stored, preserving the invariant count <= capacity.

practise.guidedTask: State the invariant before and after a successful and failed push.
practise.independentTask: Review a linked-list insertion function and document its pointer invariants and failure cleanup.
hints: Write invariants in terms that can be checked before and after every operation.
Test empty, full and one-past-capacity cases.
Use sanitizers and assertions during development where appropriate.
